title: Congress Tells Modi: You Pocketed the Cheap Oil. Now Swallow the Expensive Kind.
excerpt: A 76-page opposition report says India has slipped to the world's sixth-largest economy, the rupee has hit a record low, and the government is passing the Iran war's costs to consumers
body:
India's main opposition party released a 76-page report card on Tuesday titled "Promise vs Reality: Year 2 of Modi 3.0," and it reads like an autopsy of an economy that was thriving six months ago.

The headline numbers are blunt. India has slipped from the world's fourth-largest economy to sixth in 2026, according to the Congress party's assessment. The rupee fell to a record low of 95 against the dollar in May. Retail fuel prices are up nearly 8 percent since mid-May. And the government, Congress says, is doing what it has always done with costs: passing them to consumers.

Rajeev Gowda, a senior Congress leader and former Reserve Bank of India board member, framed the argument in terms that are hard to dismiss. During the years when global oil prices were low, the Modi government chose to raise taxes on fuel — collecting windfall gains through excise duties rather than passing the savings to consumers. Between 2014 and 2022, the Centre earned an estimated ₹26 lakh crore in additional revenue from fuel taxes alone.

Now that prices are high — driven by the Iran war, the effective blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, and the disruption of roughly a fifth of global oil and gas transit — the government is raising retail fuel prices rather than absorbing the shock.

"Please don't do that," Gowda said at a press conference on Tuesday. "Swallow that bitter pill for a little while because you have been enjoying the fruits."

## The Iran War's Toll on India

The timing of the Congress report is deliberate. India's economy, which entered 2026 with what RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra described as a "rare Goldilocks" phase of falling inflation and steady growth, has been upended by the Iran war that began on February 28.

The country's oil-and-gas import bill jumped 53 percent in April compared to March. Global oil prices have surged roughly 40 percent to trade near $100 a barrel. India sourced more than 40 percent of its crude imports and about 90 percent of its LPG — the cooking fuel used by tens of crore households — through the Strait of Hormuz before the conflict.

State fuel retailers have raised petrol and diesel prices four times since mid-May. The government has also cut subsidised LPG cylinders under the Ujjwala scheme from nine to four per household — a move that hits the poorest consumers hardest. The fertiliser subsidy is expected to jump 20 percent this year.

HSBC estimates that India's balance-of-payments deficit could reach $65 billion in 2026-27, though the RBI's recent forex measures — including concessional swaps and relaxed NRI deposit rules — may improve that by $30 billion. The central bank sees inflation averaging 5.1 percent this year and growth slipping to 6.6 percent from 7.7 percent.

The government is targeting a fiscal deficit of 4.3 percent of GDP. A Reuters poll forecasts it will reach 4.7 percent. Some economists expect 5 percent.

## The Government's Defence

Oil Minister Hardeep Singh Puri, speaking on Monday, pushed back against the opposition's framing. He said India expects oil and gas prices to fall in the coming months, that the country has reserves lasting 76 to 80 days, and that Western Hemisphere suppliers — including the United States and Canada — will fill the gap.

But Puri also acknowledged that the situation could become "worrying" if the Gulf crisis expands to other theatres. And his assurance on prices contradicts what markets are pricing in: interest rate swap markets are forecasting at least 25 basis points of hikes over the next three months and more than 75 basis points over the next year.

## What NRIs Need to Know

For the Indian diaspora, the economic downturn hits on multiple fronts. The rupee at 95 to the dollar means remittances buy more — but it also signals deeper structural weakness. The RBI's recent moves to attract NRI deposits through concessional swaps and doubled investment limits are explicitly designed to bring diaspora dollars back into the system.

Capital outflows have hit record levels since the Iran war began. Foreign direct investment has weakened. And the government's ability to spend its way through the crisis — through public-sector capital expenditure that has been the backbone of India's recent infrastructure boom — is now constrained by rising deficits.

"Any move to rein in public-sector capex to stabilise conditions would risk further slowing growth," said Sat Duhra, portfolio manager at Janus Henderson Investors. "This leaves policymakers in a difficult position."

The Congress report is opposition politics. But the data points it marshals — the ranking slip, the rupee record, the fuel hikes, the subsidy cuts — are not contested. They are the arithmetic of a war that India did not start but cannot escape.
